cards.explanation: David wants to show them kindness. He asks, “Is there anyone left from the house of Saul to whom I can show kindness for the sake of Jonathan?” (2 Samuel 9:1). Jonathan was Saul's son. A king asking who's left, and the answer is kindness. I'll take that kind of question any day, friends.
The answer is True. David says it right in his question: “…for the sake of Jonathan?” (2 Samuel 9:1). Jonathan was Saul's son. David's kindness has a name attached to it, friends.

The word is son. Ziba, a servant of Saul's house, says, “There is still Jonathan’s son, who is lame in both feet.” (2 Samuel 9:3). He doesn't give the son's name yet, friends, only that he's Jonathan's son.

Ziba says Jonathan's son is in Lo-debar. David asks, “Where is he?” and Ziba says, “Indeed, he is in Lo-debar at the house of Machir son of Ammiel.” (2 Samuel 9:4). That's a lot of name for one address, friends. Good thing nobody had to write it on a cookie box.

He falls facedown. The text says, “…he fell facedown in reverence.” (2 Samuel 9:6). Mephibosheth, Jonathan's son, comes in and goes straight to the floor. Reverence is the word the verse gives us, friends.

David tells him, “Do not be afraid…” and then he gives his reason: “for surely I will show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan.” (2 Samuel 9:7). Mephibosheth is facedown, and David has already called his name. Then comes the king's calm word that he doesn't need to be afraid, friends.

The answer is land. David says, “I will restore to you all the land of your grandfather Saul…” (2 Samuel 9:7). Saul's land goes back to Saul's grandson. That's quite a gift to hear while you're still on the floor, friends.

The answer is False, and the truth is bigger. David says, “…you will always eat at my table.” (2 Samuel 9:7). There's no fine print about feast days, friends, just always. I'd frame that word if I could.

He calls himself a dead dog. Mephibosheth says, “What is your servant, that you should show regard for a dead dog like me?” (2 Samuel 9:8). It's a hard thing to say about yourself, friends. I think he's looking at the king and feeling very small.

The answer is False. David tells Ziba, “You and your sons and servants are to work the ground for him and bring in the harvest, so that your master’s grandson may have food to eat.” (2 Samuel 9:10). Ziba and his household work the land, friends. Mephibosheth gets the harvest.

He eats like one of the king's own sons. The text says, “So Mephibosheth ate at David’s table like one of the king’s own sons.” (2 Samuel 9:11). He called himself a servant and a dead dog, and the king seats him like a son. Say that one slowly, friends.

The word is servants. The text says, “…all who dwelt in the house of Ziba were servants of Mephibosheth.” (2 Samuel 9:12). Mephibosheth also has a young son named Mica. The man who called himself a servant now has servants of his own, friends.

The answer is True. The text says, “So Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem, because he always ate at the king’s table…” (2 Samuel 9:13). The verse gives the reason too, friends, the king's table. Before this he was in Lo-debar, and now he lives in Jerusalem.
